items.heading: Treating a Bigger Shortlist As
items.text: Treating a bigger shortlist as more thorough research. Once a choice set grows past a handful of live options, added research on choice overload has found decision confidence tends to fall, not rise - more names on the list is more weight to carry, not more clarity gained.

items.heading: Scoring Appeal Before Applying Hard
items.text: Scoring appeal before applying hard constraints. Falling for an option before checking whether it clears your basic constraints means you now have to break your own heart to drop it - screen for constraints first and appeal has nothing left to attach to unfairly.

items.heading: Letting Years Already Invested Make
items.text: Letting years already invested make the decision for you. Sunk-cost reasoning treats time and money already spent as if they were still a reason to continue, when the only real question is which option is the better bet from today forward, regardless of what it cost to get here.

items.heading: Setting an Intention Instead
items.text: Setting an intention instead of a specific plan. "I will decide by the end of the month" without a specific date, a specific next action, and a specific trigger rarely gets kept. A vague goal and a bound plan feel similar to write down and behave completely differently in practice.

items.heading: Whether the Option You Grabbed
items.text: Whether the option you grabbed under pressure survives contact with a real constraint - money, family, or a fixed timeline - once you are already six months in.

items.heading: Whether You Actually Compared IT
items.text: Whether you actually compared it against your other real options, or just picked whichever one happened to come up first.

items.heading: Whether the Appeal Was Ever
items.text: Whether the appeal was ever tested against the real day-to-day work, or only against the idea of the work.
